delivery: low, ominous, then a hard punch on 'spoiling everything'
text: October 2026. After three decades, Street Fighter is back on the big screen. And in its final act, a demon walks down off a mountain, steps into the arena, and finishes the tournament's champion in a matter of seconds. If you haven't seen the movie yet, this is your last warning. Because today, we are spoiling everything.

Welcome back to Don't Spoil It RG. This is Street Fighter, directed by Kitao Sakurai, from Legendary and Paramount. We're breaking down the beginning, every major fight, the plot twists, the ending, and the credits scene. And we're keeping two things separate: what actually happens on screen, and what's only fan theory about a sequel. Whenever we cross into theory, you'll see it flagged on screen.

delivery: quick, rhythmic, like an announcer reading a fight card
text: Quick roster check. Andrew Koji is Ryu. Noah Centineo is Ken. Callina Liang is Chun-Li. David Dastmalchian is M. Bison, and Roman Reigns, credited as Joe Anoa'i, is Akuma. Jason Momoa plays Blanka, Cody Rhodes is Guile, 50 Cent is Balrog, Vidyut Jammwal is Dhalsim, and Orville Peck is Vega. Quick note: our animated versions are drawn from the classic arcade designs, not the actors.

delivery: storyteller, nostalgic, darkening toward Gouken's death
text: The story opens in 1987, in Thailand, at the very first World Warrior Tournament. A young Ryu fights his way to the final against the giant Muay Thai king, Sagat, and wins. But not cleanly. To win, Ryu lets something dark into his fighting, and the film treats those inner demons as literally real. That surge of killing intent reaches someone who has been waiting for it: Akuma. In the aftermath, Ryu's master, Gouken, is killed by Akuma. And Ryu walks away from everything. His title. His training. His best friend, Ken.

delivery: brisk, a little wry about Ken
text: Six years later, in 1993, the two have drifted apart. Ryu is living in self-imposed exile, wandering, barely fighting at all. Ken Masters went the other way. He's a showman now, a fighter for the cameras, all flash and no real stakes. Then Chun-Li shows up. She needs both of them inside a brand-new event: the second World Warrior Tournament. And the old wound between Ryu and Ken tears open the second they're in the same room.

delivery: reveal energy, then quiet sincerity on her father
text: Here's the first big reveal. Chun-Li isn't just a fighter. She's an undercover Interpol agent, and this isn't just a job for her. It's personal. M. Bison killed her father. She's been working her way toward him for years, and this tournament is the closest she has ever gotten.

Because the tournament is a front. Bison, played by David Dastmalchian, is running a scheme for global domination, and what he wants is power. More Psycho Power than any human has ever held. His operation drains Hado energy from fighters, so gathering the strongest warriors on the planet in one place is basically building himself a buffet. But the fighters are only the appetizer. The real target is the most dangerous dark power on Earth: Akuma. And the one person who can draw Akuma down from his mountain is Ryu.

Before a single official match, the fighters collide in a nightclub. Ken, Ryu, Guile, Dhalsim, Vega and Balrog all end up in one glorious, ridiculous brawl. It's the movie at its most fun, and Cody Rhodes' Guile gets some of the funniest lines in the film.

Then comes the tournament proper. Honestly, it gets less screen time than a lot of fans hoped, only a handful of bouts. But Ken makes them count. He takes down Balrog, 50 Cent's heavyweight boxer. Then he beats Dhalsim. Suddenly the showman is one win away from the title, and for the first time in years, he's fighting like he actually means it.

Ryu, meanwhile, never makes it to his match. Bison captures him. And to force Ryu's power to the surface, Bison makes him fight Blanka, played by Jason Momoa, feral and crackling with electricity, while he watches the dark energy start to rise.

delivery: quiet, heavy, emotional; let the confession land
text: Now the movie's emotional twist. The reason Ryu and Ken fell apart wasn't just Ryu disappearing. Ryu finally confesses that back in 1987, jealousy drove him to sabotage Ken's shot at that first tournament. That's the secret he's carried for six years. And in the fight that follows, Ryu beats Ken anyway. Ken never makes it to the final.

delivery: build tension slowly, then go cold and quiet on the death
text: Which leads to the cruelest beat in the film. Promoter Don Sauvage, played by Eric André, is thrilled that Ken is a no-show, and he declares Joe, played by UFC champion Alexander Volkanovski, the winner by forfeit. Joe only got this far because Ryu, his original opponent, was captured. And then Akuma descends from his mountain and challenges the new champion. Seconds later, Joe is down. And it seems, he's dead.

Ryu arrives and challenges Akuma alone. And he can't win clean. So he does the one thing he swore he'd never do again. He lets the hatred in. This is Evil Ryu, the version longtime fans know from the games. Evil Ryu beats Akuma. But the darkness doesn't switch off. Ryu turns on his own friends.

Then comes the payoff the whole movie has been building to. Ken, the one who never could, plants his feet, cups his hands, and finally throws a real Hadouken. It hits Ryu and snaps him back to himself.

But while the heroes were fighting each other, Bison collected the real prize. His men restrain the unconscious Akuma and haul him away. Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li and Dan chase after them, until Cammy destroys their vehicle. Bison escapes. With Akuma.

So here's where the movie lands. Bison is free, and the most dangerous fighter alive is his prisoner. Akuma is not dead. And notice what the film doesn't show: we never actually see Bison extract Akuma's power. That's being saved for later. Meanwhile, Guile and Dhalsim pick up our heroes, and Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li and Dan hit the road together to hunt Bison down. A lot of viewers found that ending abrupt. The movie builds Bison up as the big bad, then spends its climax on Akuma. But it's clearly designed to leave the door wide open.

delivery: hushed, conspiratorial, then a satisfied reveal on 'Sagat'
text: And stay in your seat, because there's an animated credits scene. Some outlets call it mid-credits, others post-credits, so watch all the way through. Somewhere tropical, Bison and his lieutenants approach a towering man with an eyepatch and a huge scar across his chest. It's Sagat, the man Ryu defeated back in 1987. And Bison is here to offer him an alliance.

Let's lock in what's confirmed. Chun-Li is Interpol, out to avenge her father. Ryu sabotaged Ken back in 1987. Akuma killed Gouken, and Joe appears to die. Ryu became Evil Ryu and came back thanks to Ken's Hadouken. Bison escaped with Akuma alive. And Sagat is now in Bison's sights.

Now, theory time. None of this is confirmed, and no sequel had been officially announced when we made this video. Theory one: Bison drains Akuma and becomes something far beyond human. Theory two: Sagat joins Bison out of revenge, setting up Ryu versus Sagat, round two. Theory three: Ryu's dark side isn't gone, it's just sleeping. Theory four: Gouken could come back, because in the games, he survived Akuma. And theory five: Cammy, Zangief, E. Honda and the rest finally get real arcs next time.
So what did you think? Did the ending land, or did it feel rushed? Tell me in the comments, hit subscribe, and remember: on this channel, we spoil it so you don't have to. See you next round.
